newsitem.title: UK: Police, Orangemen meet on vexed N.Ireland marches.
newsitem.headline: Police, Orangemen meet on vexed N.Ireland marches.

text.p: Giles Elgood
Northern Ireland's police chief met leaders of the Protestant Orange Order on Thursday in a bid to defuse the threat of violence hanging over their weekend parades through Catholic enclaves.

Ronnie Flanagan, head of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, had talks with the Orangemen and Lord Molyneaux, a former Orange leader and onetime head of the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, 48 hours before parades in Belfast and Londonderry.
"Senior officers continue to be engaged in discussions with those of influence throughout the community in an effort to seek a resolution to the current parades issue," a police spokesman said.
There was no immediate indication of whether Flanagan had managed to persuade the Orange leaders to divert their march from Belfast's Catholic Lower Ormeau Road.

In Washington, U.S. congressman Joseph Kennedy joined calls urging that Orange Order marches should be banned along disputed routes in Northern Ireland, a British province plagued by sectarian conflict for decades.

"The resolution sends a clear and simple message to the British government and to Prime Minister Tony Blair: Orange Order marches should be banned along disputed routes," Kennedy said. Such parades "only serve to inflame tensions and further undermine the fragile peace process", he added.
An Orange march along the Catholic Garvaghy Road in Portadown last Sunday sparked some of the worst Irish nationalist violence in Northern Ireland for many years.

Police on Thursday blew up a suspicious package left outside the offices of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), the main Protestant political party which wants Northern Ireland to stay British, unlike Catholic republicans.
An uneasy calm appeared to have settled on the province in the run-up to the weekend. "There's not much to report. The city's quiet," a Belfast police spokesman said.
John Taylor, a senior member of the UUP, dismissed a suggestion that the Orange Order should take the high ground and call off its parades as "nationalist propaganda".
An Orange Order spokesman added: "We are all fearful of what might happen, but we want the parade to pass off peacefully."
For Orangemen, Saturday is the "glorious" 12th of July, the climax of an annual marching season when Orangemen stage parades to mark the 1690 Protestant battlefield victory over a Catholic King.
The Orange Order was reported by political sources to be under intense pressure to modify its proposed marches down Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road and in the city centre of Londonderry.

The centuries-old Order says it is being wrongly blamed for the violence that flared after Sunday's march along the Garvaghy Road and wants only to hold peaceful marches to celebrate its Protestant faith and British loyalty.
Nationalist spokesmen called for peaceful demonstrations in protest against the Orange marches.
Catholic leaders urged their supporters to turn up in their thousands to prevent what they see as sectarian, triumphalist parades on their doorsteps on Saturday.

A sports club near the Lower Ormeau Road was partly destroyed in what police said was an arson attack on Wednesday evening. Stones were thrown at a bus carrying nationalists back from a demonstration and three women were hurt.
The general level of violence has subsided in the last few days but security forces were braced for more unrest.
"It's much quieter. But I get the feeling it's only half time," said one security source.
Britain said it was sending between 400 and 500 more troops to the province to "combat terrorism and help maintain law and order" and back up police in the front line against the unrest.
